description: We are a team of engineering students driven by the vision of standing out through new ideas and projects that contribute to building a better world. As first-time participants in an event of this caliber, our goal is to inspire confidence and trust. We want to show that you don't need to be a top student to participate and succeed—you just need the courage to try. Success is only one step away from fear.
summary:
AgroSpace is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers explore, simulate, and compare crop rotation strategies using NASA satellite data. Built in Python/Streamlit, it integrates three modules: a Tactical Map that analyzes slopes, runoff, and erosion risk from the SRTM digital elevation model; a Bio-Climatic Radar that cross-references soil moisture (SMAP/GLDAS), thermal stress (ECOSTRESS), and vegetation vigor (Sentinel-2 NDVI) to issue actionable alerts; and a Climate Time Machine that projects local climate up to 15 years ahead (NASA POWER historical data + CMIP6 scenarios) and simulates the impact of each rotation on nitrogen, organic matter, pests, and water.

The prototype compares the farmer’s current practice against rotations with nitrogen-fixing legumes and cover crops, backed by transparent scientific justification. Its key finding: under severe climate scenarios, cover crops stop being a cost and become the farm’s resilience insurance.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

AgroSpace is a web-based decision-support tool that lets farmers explore, simulate, and compare crop rotation strategies using NASA satellite data. It works through three modules integrated in a single interface. The Tactical Maptakes the SRTM elevation model and computes slopes, runoff accumulation, and erosion risk for the field. The Bio-Climatic Radar cross-references root-zone soil moisture (SMAP/GLDAS), land surface temperature (ECOSTRESS), and vegetation vigor (Sentinel-2 NDVI) into a vulnerability index that issues actionable alerts. The Climate Time Machine projects local climate up to 15 years ahead by combining NASA POWER historical data with CMIP6 scenarios, then runs an annual soil simulator on that projection, where yield depends on four interpretable factors: water, nitrogen, pest pressure, and organic matter. Three strategies—the farmer’s current practice, a rotation with nitrogen-fixing legumes, and one with cover crops—are compared on the same climate, so the only thing that changes is the human decision.

What are its benefits?

It turns complex satellite data into a concrete answer: what to plant, in what order, and why. Every recommendation comes with its scientific justification (water savings, nitrogen fixed, pest cycle disruption, erosion reduction), giving the farmer evidence rather than just a suggestion. It requires no credentials or special hardware and, if connectivity drops, switches to a demo mode with plausible data so work is never interrupted.

What is the intended impact?

In our simulations, moving from monoculture to a legume-and-cover-crop rotation cuts the cumulative water deficit five-fold over ten years and fixes up to 120 kg of nitrogen per hectare without fertilizer. The most important finding is that the recommendation changes with the severity of the climate scenario: under mild conditions the highest-income rotation wins, but under severe scenarios cover crops stop being a cost and become the farm’s resilience insurance. That is exactly the conversation we want to enable on small and medium farms in semi-arid regions.

Tools and technologies

Python 3.10 with Streamlit for the web interface; pandas and NumPy for data processing and the simulation engine; Plotly for interactive, animated charts; Folium for the satellite map; requests for the NASA POWER REST client; rasterio and GeoPandas for raster and vector data. Data sources are SMAP, ECOSTRESS, SRTM, NASA POWER/GLDAS, and Sentinel-2 (ESA). The code is modular and open for anyone to use.

How is the project creative?

It unifies three time scales in one cockpit: the terrain’s past, the crop’s present, and the climate’s future. The Radar introduces a drought × heat interaction term, because the physiological double hit is worse than the sum of its parts. And the Time Machine turns an agronomic model into a visual experience where strategies draw themselves year by year and the recommendation recalculates live as you move the climate scenario.

What factors did the team consider?

We prioritized scientific transparency over black boxes: every factor in the model can be explained. We designed for non-technical users with questions in a farmer’s language, and for judges with methodological references (FAO-56, RUSLE, Horn 1981). We built in robustness through graceful degradation when APIs fail, and fairness in comparison by simulating all strategies on the same projected climate.
dataRefs: ECOSTRESS – ECOsystem Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment (NASA/JPL)
NASA POWER – Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources
GLDAS – Global Land Data Assimilation System (NASA Goddard)
Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (acceso a Sentinel-2)
NASA Earthdata (acceso unificado a datos NASA)
